excerpt: How a web page is broken into packets, addressed, carried, and put back together, and what an IP address and a port actually are.

body.text: This lesson explains TCP/IP in ordinary words: how a message leaves your device, gets split up, travels, and arrives. You will learn what an IP address is, what a port does, and why a page sometimes loads in pieces.
TCP/IP is the set of rules that lets different machines talk. IP moves small pieces across the network, and TCP makes sure the pieces arrive and are put back in order.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
A browser, so you can watch the ideas happen.

body.text: The address, and why it has two parts

items: An IP address identifies a device on a network, such as 102.89.33.7.
Your home router gives your laptop an address that begins 192.168, which is private.
The public address is the one the outside world sees, shared by everything at home.
The address alone reaches a machine, not a service on that machine.
A port number names the service, such as 443 for secure web pages.
So an address plus a port points at one specific door on one specific machine.

body.text: You will see this in your browser's developer tools, where each request shows a host and a port. Most are hidden from you, usually 443, which is why the address bar shows only the name.

body.alt: Parcels on a road, each labelled with an address and a number.
body.caption: Each packet carries the address, the port, and its place in the sequence. The labels are what make reassembly possible.

body.text: It looks like a message travels as one piece, like a letter. A page is broken into many small packets, and each one may take a different route.
What happens when you open a page

items: You type a name, and the device asks a name service for the matching IP address.
That lookup is DNS, which works like a phone book for names.
The device opens a connection to the address on port 443.
It sends a request, and the server replies with the page in packets.
Each packet is numbered, and the receiving device acknowledges the ones it got.
Missing packets are sent again, and the page appears once enough of it has arrived.

body.text: A slow page that shows text first and pictures later is this process working. The parts arrive in an order the browser can draw, and the heavy parts follow.

body.alt: A router with several cables and small indicator lights.
body.caption: The router holds the private addresses and shares one public address. The lights show packets moving, not pages.

body.text: TCP and UDP, in one paragraph each
TCP checks that everything arrived and asks again for what did not. It is slower and reliable, which is what a web page and a bank transfer need.
UDP sends without waiting for confirmation. It is faster and drops packets when the network is busy, which suits a live call where an old sound is useless.

items: Web pages use TCP, because a missing piece breaks the page.
Email uses TCP, because a missing line matters.
Video calls often use UDP, because waiting is worse than a glitch.
Online games usually use UDP, for the same reason.
File downloads use TCP, because a corrupt file is a failure.
Neither is better. Each matches the job.

body.text: None of this needs a network qualification to use. It explains why a call freezes but continues, while a download stops and restarts.
Do not worry about memorising the numbers. Two facts carry most of the value: addresses find machines, and ports find services.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a common symptom, and each points at a different layer.

items: The name does not resolve: DNS is failing, and typing the IP address directly sometimes works.
The page loads without pictures: some packets are lost repeatedly, which suggests a weak signal.
One site fails and others work: the problem is at that site or on the route to it.
Everything fails: check the router, then the provider, before changing any settings.
A call freezes but keeps going: that is UDP dropping packets, and it recovers by itself.
A download stops at ninety per cent: the connection dropped, and the retry starts again.

body.text: Practice
Watch the process once, and it stops being abstract.

items: Open a page and note how the text appears before the images.
Find your device's IP address in the network settings.
Find the router's private address, usually ending in .1.
Use a speed test and note the difference between download and upload.
Turn the wifi off mid-load and watch the page stop and resume.

body.text: You can now picture how the network carries a message. In the next lesson you will see what a digital signature proves, and what it does not.

excerpt: What a digital signature actually proves, how the padlock in a browser works, and why a signed PDF is not the same as a scanned signature.

body.text: This lesson explains what a digital signature proves and what it does not. You will learn how the padlock in a browser works, how a signed PDF differs from a scanned signature, and the one thing a signature never confirms.

A digital signature uses mathematics to show two things: the document has not changed since it was signed, and it came from the holder of a particular key. It says nothing about whether the signer meant what they signed.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
A browser, to look at a padlock.

body.text: The padlock, step by step

items: The site sends you a certificate, which is a file naming the site and its public key.
The certificate is signed by an authority that your browser already trusts.
The browser checks that signature, and checks the name matches the site.
It also checks the certificate has not expired or been withdrawn.
If all three pass, the padlock appears, and the connection is encrypted.
If any check fails, the browser shows a warning, which you should never ignore.

body.text: You will see the padlock at the left of the address, and clicking it opens a short panel naming the organisation that issued the certificate. A padlock with no organisation named is worth a second look on a bank page.

body.alt: A browser panel showing certificate details and the issuing authority.
body.caption: The certificate names the site and the authority that issued it. The padlock confirms the connection, not the honesty of the business.

body.text: It looks like a padlock means the site is safe to trust with money. It means the connection is private and the name is confirmed, and a dishonest shop can have both.
What a signature on a file proves

items: The file has not changed by even one character since signing.
The signing key belongs to the person or organisation named in the certificate.
The time of signing was recorded by the service that issued the key.
Nothing else. It does not prove the signer read the document.
It does not prove the signer had authority to sign it.
It does not prove the contents are true.

body.text: A signed PDF will show a coloured band at the top naming the signer and the date. Click the band and the details open, including whether the document has been changed since.

body.alt: A document with a wax-style seal beside a laptop showing a signature panel.
body.caption: A seal proves the document was closed by a particular hand. A digital signature proves the same thing, and also that nothing was altered afterwards.

body.text: The scanned signature is not a signature
A picture of a signature pasted into a document proves nothing at all. It can be copied from any earlier letter, and it carries no check on the document's contents.

items: A scanned signature is an image, and images are copied in seconds.
A digital signature is tied to the exact file, so any change breaks it.
For a bank or a court, the digital version is the stronger evidence.
For an ordinary letter, a scanned signature is accepted as a courtesy, not as proof.
If you must use a scan, keep the original document and the email trail.
For anything with money or property attached, ask for the digital version.

body.text: None of this requires special software to check. Any modern PDF reader shows whether a signature is valid in one click.
Do not worry if you have signed things by scanning. Most offices accept it, and knowing the difference is what protects you in the few cases that matter.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a warning worth understanding, and none of them is a reason to panic.

items: The padlock is missing on a bank page: leave it, and type the address yourself next time.
The certificate has expired: the site owner has not renewed it. Treat it as a stop sign.
The signature band says the document was changed: ask for a fresh copy before acting.
The signer's name looks wrong: check the certificate details, not only the display name.
A PDF signature will not validate on your reader: update the reader before assuming fraud.
An email claims to be signed: look for the badge in the mail app, not a picture in the message.

body.text: Practice
Look at one certificate properly, which teaches more than a definition.

items: Open a bank site and click the padlock.
Read the organisation name and the issuer.
Check the expiry date.
Open a news site and compare its certificate.
Note one difference between the two.

body.text: You can now read a padlock and know what it is telling you. In the next lesson you will see what a frontend developer actually builds.

excerpt: What a frontend developer builds, the three languages involved, why the same page looks different on a phone, and how a beginner starts.

body.text: This lesson explains the frontend developer's job: the part of a website you can see and touch. You will learn the three languages involved, why a page must work on a small screen, and the first steps for somebody starting today.
The frontend is everything that runs in your browser. The backend, by contrast, runs on a server and holds the data, and the two talk to each other over the network.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
A browser, and curiosity about how a page is made.

body.text: The three languages

items: HTML gives the page its structure: headings, paragraphs, forms, and images.
CSS gives it appearance: colours, spacing, size, and where things sit.
JavaScript gives it behaviour: what happens when you click, type, or scroll.
A page with only HTML works and looks plain.
A page with CSS looks finished but does nothing.
A page with JavaScript can respond, calculate, and load new information.

body.text: You will see all three in a browser: right-click a page and choose Inspect, and the panel shows the structure on one side and the styles on the other. That panel is the developer's main tool, and it is free.

body.alt: A code editor beside a browser showing a web page being built.
body.caption: Code on one side, the result on the other. A beginner can start with two files and one browser tab.

body.text: It looks like a developer memorises the whole language before building anything. Most of the work is looking things up, and the skill is knowing what to look for.
The same page, three screens

items: A page built for a laptop often breaks on a phone, with text too small and buttons too close.
Responsive design means one page that rearranges itself for the screen size.
The browser reports its width, and the styles choose a layout to fit.
Test at three widths: a phone, a tablet, and a laptop.
Check that buttons are big enough for a thumb, not only a mouse.
Check the page on a slow connection, since most visitors are on one.

body.text: The layout will change as you drag the window narrower, with columns folding into one. That change is the whole point, and it happens without a second version of the site.

body.alt: The same web page shown on a phone and a laptop screen.
body.caption: One page, two layouts. The content is identical, and only the arrangement changes with the width.

body.text: A day in the job

items: Read the design and the ticket, then ask what happens on a small screen.
Build the structure first, and check it works without styling.
Add the styling, and compare with the design.
Add the behaviour, and test the awkward cases: empty fields, slow network, long names.
Fix what the reviewer finds, and write a short note on what changed.
Deploy, then look at the page on a real phone rather than only the browser tool.

body.text: None of this needs a degree. A portfolio of three working pages, each solving a real problem, counts for more than a certificate alone.
Do not worry about the frameworks with unfamiliar names. They change every few years, and the three languages underneath do not.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a normal part of building, not a sign that you cannot do it.

items: The page looks wrong in one browser: check the console for errors before changing the styles.
A button does nothing: the script has an error, or the element name does not match.
The layout breaks on a phone: a fixed width was used. Replace it with a flexible one.
The page is slow: large images are the usual cause. Shrink them before anything else.
Your changes do not appear: the browser cached the old file. Reload with the cache cleared.
You copied code you do not understand: rewrite one line at a time until it makes sense.

body.text: Practice
Build one page this week, even an ugly one.

items: Create a file with a heading, two paragraphs, and a link.
Open it in a browser and read it on a phone as well.
Add a colour and a font size in a style block.
Add a button that shows a message when clicked.
Right-click and inspect one element, and change its colour in the panel.

body.text: You can now see the work behind a page you use. In the next lesson you will see what a machine learning engineer builds.

excerpt: What a machine learning engineer actually does with data, how a model is trained and tested, and the questions that decide whether it works.

body.text: This lesson explains the machine learning engineer's work: collecting examples, training a model, testing it honestly, and running it where people use it. You will learn the steps and the questions that decide whether the result is useful.
A model is a program that learns patterns from examples rather than following rules written by hand. The engineer's job is to choose the examples, test the result, and watch it after release.
Before you start

items: About twenty-five minutes.
No mathematics required for this description.

body.text: The steps, in order

items: Define the question: what decision will this model help somebody make?
Collect examples of inputs and the correct answers, which is the training data.
Clean the data, since missing values and duplicates mislead the training.
Split the examples, keeping some back for testing later.
Train the model on one part, and check it on the part kept back.
Deploy it, then watch what happens with real users.

body.text: You will see a training run print a score that improves and then levels off, often with a chart. The level-off is the point where more training stops helping, and the engineer then looks at the data instead.

body.alt: A screen showing training charts with accuracy rising and then flattening.
body.caption: Accuracy rises and then flattens. Past that point the problem is the data, not the amount of training.

body.text: It looks like a high score means the model is ready. A high score on the training examples can hide a model that has memorised them and learned nothing.
Testing that tells the truth

items: Test on examples the model never saw, which is why the data was split.
Compare against a simple rule, since a model that loses to a rule is not ready.
Check the errors rather than only the total, because some mistakes cost far more.
Check performance by group, so one kind of user is not served badly.
Test on data from a different month, since a model can go stale quickly.
Write down what the model cannot do, which is the part people forget.

body.text: The test results will show a confusion table: correct and incorrect answers in each direction. Reading the table takes a minute and says more than one summary number.
Ask for the table rather than the score, whenever somebody shows you a model. Once you can read it, you can tell whether the tool is useful for your problem.

body.alt: A whiteboard with a diagram of data flowing into a model and out to users.
body.caption: The diagram is the design: data in, model in the middle, decisions out, and a way to watch the results.

body.text: Where the job is hardest

items: Data collection, which is slow and mostly manual.
Labelling, which needs somebody expert in the subject.
Keeping the model current as the world changes.
Explaining a decision to a customer who was refused.
Watching for silent failures after release, when nothing crashes but answers are wrong.
Deciding when not to use a model at all, which is a common and correct answer.

body.text: None of this replaces the people who know the work. The engineer builds the tool, and the nurse, the loan officer, or the teacher decides what to do with its answer.
If you are considering the career, start with the data rather than the model. You will learn more from cleaning a messy table of real records than from reading about a new technique.
Do not worry about the mathematics if you are only curious. The judgement questions above are the ones that decide whether a project helps anybody.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a known failure, and each is found by testing rather than guessing.

items: The model is accurate in testing and wrong in use: the test data did not match real users.
The model refuses one group more often: check the training examples for that group.
The output changed after an update: a data source changed its format.
Nobody trusts the tool: the decisions were never explained to the people affected.
The training takes days: the data is too large or the settings too ambitious.
The model works but nobody uses it: the question was interesting and the workflow was not.

body.text: Practice
Think through one small problem, without writing code.

items: Choose a decision made often in a business you know.
Write down what inputs a person uses to make it.
Write what a correct answer looks like.
Name one case where a wrong answer would be expensive.
Decide whether a rule of thumb would do the job, and why.

body.text: You can now describe the work without the mystique. In the next lesson you will see how teams organise the building itself.

excerpt: How agile teams plan in short cycles, what a stand-up is for, and how DevOps gets a change safely into use without a weekend of panic.

body.text: This lesson explains agile and DevOps in ordinary words: how a team decides what to build next, and how a change reaches users without breaking things. You will learn the meetings, the board, and the pipeline that catches mistakes early.
Agile is a way of working in short cycles with frequent review. DevOps is the habit of building, testing, and releasing automatically, so a small change can go out safely on a Tuesday.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
Any experience of a team project, which is enough.

body.text: The short cycle

items: The team keeps a list of work, called the backlog, in order of value.
It chooses a small amount for the next two weeks, which is the sprint.
Each day it meets for fifteen minutes to say what moved and what is stuck.
At the end it shows working software to the people who asked for it.
It then reviews how it worked, and changes one thing for the next cycle.
Anything unfinished goes back to the list rather than being declared done.

body.text: You will see a board with three columns: to do, doing, and done. Cards move across during the sprint, and a card that sits in doing for a week is the useful signal.

body.alt: A board with three columns of sticky notes and a team standing beside it.
body.caption: The board is the plan, and anyone can read it. A crowded doing column means the team started too much at once.

body.text: It looks like the daily meeting exists to report to a manager. It exists so the team finds its own blockers before they cost a day.
The pipeline

items: A developer sends a change for review, and a colleague reads it.
Automated tests run on the change, and a failure stops it.
A build is created and deployed to a test environment automatically.
Somebody checks the change on a test copy, ideally the person who asked for it.
It is released to users, often gradually, so a problem affects few people first.
Monitoring watches the error rate, and a jump means a rollback.

body.text: The pipeline screen will show each stage as a tick or a cross, with the failing step in red. That one screen tells you whether the change is safe before anybody sees it.

body.alt: A screen showing a deployment pipeline with stages marked as passed or failed.
body.caption: Each stage is a gate. A red cross stops the change, and the fix happens before users are affected.

body.text: Why small releases are safer
Ask your team one question this week: how long would it take to undo the last release? If nobody knows the answer, you have found the first thing to fix.

items: A small change is quick to understand and quick to reverse.
A large change hides several problems in one release.
Releasing often means each release is boring, which is the goal.
A rollback is a decision, not a crisis, when it has been practised.
Users report problems faster when a change is small enough to name.
The team stops saving work for a big weekend event that fails.

body.text: None of this needs a large company. Two people with a shared board and one automated test already have the essentials.
If your team has no board, you can start one with paper and a wall. You will be surprised how much arguing stops once the work is visible to everybody.
Do not worry about the vocabulary of ceremonies and artefacts. The board, the short cycle, the review, and the automatic test are the parts that change the work.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is common, and each has a correction the team can make itself.

items: The sprint ends with nothing finished: the team took on too much. Take less next time.
The board is not updated: nobody trusts it, so the meeting becomes the plan instead.
Every release breaks something: the tests do not cover the parts being changed.
Reviews take days: the changes are too large. Smaller changes get read.
The stand-up runs for forty minutes: it has become a status report. Take it offline.
Deployment is done by hand at midnight: that is the problem to fix first.

body.text: Practice
Run one short cycle on any project, paid or unpaid.

items: Write five tasks on cards and put them in one column.
Choose two for this week, and move them to doing.
Meet yourself for five minutes each morning to check progress.
At the end of the week, show what works to somebody.
Write one sentence on what to change next week.

body.text: You can now see how software gets built by teams. In the next lesson you will see the career that reads the numbers.
